One thing I've noticed about Web3 is that we're strangely good at adapting to bad experiences.

We complain and joke about them, but then eventually, we accept them.

➢ Switching between apps.
➢ Copying wallet addresses.
➢ Jumping from chats to wallets to feeds and back again.
➢ Missing opportunities because by the time you're ready to act, the moment has already passed.

For the longest time, I thought that was normal.

Most of us probably did.

That's why @DlicomApp caught me off guard.

Not because it promised something revolutionary, but because it made me realize how much friction I'd quietly accepted.

➫ Social feed.
➫ Encrypted messaging.
➫ Built-in wallet.
➫ Staking.
➫ Even in-chat transactions.

The surprising part wasn't seeing all of those things in one place.

The surprising part was realizing I'd spent so long accepting the opposite.

I think that's what separates good products from forgettable ones.

They don't solve the problems you're constantly talking about. 

They solve the problems you've stopped noticing.

Nobody talks about who actually suffers when a wire transfer takes four days.

It's not the person with three bank accounts and a financial advisor. They have buffers. They have credit lines. A delayed transfer is an inconvenience  annoying, not dangerous.

The person it actually hurts is the freelancer in Cairo waiting on a client payment to cover rent. The small merchant in Karachi whose supplier won't ship until funds clear. The family in Lagos sending money across a border that two different banking systems treat as suspicious by default.

For those users, "bank delays" isn't a UX complaint. It's a material problem with real consequences.

@DlicomApp's payment gateway sits inside the chat. No bank in the middle. No correspondent banking fees quietly eating 3-7% of the transfer. No four-day clearing window because two institutions need to confirm the same transaction exists. The payment and the conversation are the same interaction  and it settles when it settles, not when the infrastructure gets around to it.

The KYC piece is worth sitting with separately. KYC was designed to protect institutions from liability. It was never really designed to protect users. What it practically does is create a filter  and that filter disproportionately excludes people from exactly the regions where fast, cheap payments matter most.

A self-custody wallet with no KYC requirement doesn't eliminate fraud. But it stops treating every unbanked user as a potential criminal by default.

That's a different starting assumption. And starting assumptions matter more than features.

"Human-centered" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

Every platform that ever burned users with toxic content eventually said something similar. Facebook had a wellbeing initiative. Twitter had conversation health scores. YouTube adjusted its recommendation engine at least four times. The language was always about humans. The behavior never changed because the incentive never changed.

So when @DlicomApp says the AI feed filters toxicity  the interesting question isn't whether the technology works. It's what "filtered" actually means in practice.

There's a difference between removing toxicity and removing friction. Platforms confuse these constantly. A feed with no conflict isn't human-centered  it's just comfortable. And comfortable feeds have their own problem: they stop showing you things that challenge your thinking. The filter bubble isn't a side effect of cleaning up feeds. It's usually the direct result.

The Dlicom feed sits on top of a wallet. Tipping, staking, community activity  all of it happens in the same environment. That context matters because a financially active user behaves differently than a passive scroller. They're not just consuming they have skin in the content they engage with.

Whether the AI accounts for that difference is genuinely unclear to me.

Filtering rage bait is the easy part. Most decent moderation systems can do that. The harder problem is building a feed that keeps users genuinely engaged without manufacturing the kind of emotional friction that made old platforms so sticky in the first place.

Those are two different engineering problems. Most people asking for "less toxicity" are only thinking about the first one.

These aren't exotic vulnerabilities.

The word "audited" stopped meaning anything because projects started using it as marketing. 
Hacken's name is one of the few things that gives it weight again.

one of the main security problems in web3 isn't the blockchain, but the way users interact with different tools

in most cases, the same process requires several applications:

⤷ you see an idea in a chat 
⤷ open your wallet
⤷ navigate to an external interface
⤷ execute a transaction
⤷ return to the discussion

each of these transitions introduces additional risks: phishing links, fake interfaces or malicious contracts

more external interactions = larger attack surface

platforms like @DlicomApp are trying to solve this problem by bringing several key parts of crypto interaction into a single environment

instead of separating communication, wallets and transactions across different applications, these elements can operate within the same platform

in this model user action goes through several logical stages: 

⤷ discussion in the social environment
⤷ wallet approval
⤷ security checks
⤷ and only after that the transaction is executed and sent to the blockchain

when these steps exist within the same ecosystem, the interaction becomes more predictable and controlled

this doesn't eliminate all web3 risks, but it can significantly reduce the number of vulnerable points when interacting with crypto services
